label: Medical Ethics, Law and the Philosophy of Medicine

lessons.title: Principlism: Four Prima Facie Principles
body: Clinical ethics needs a vocabulary that clinicians, patients, lawyers and philosophers with different deep commitments can all use. The most influential candidate is principlism, set out by Tom Beauchamp and James Childress in Principles of Biomedical Ethics (first edition 1979). It proposes four mid-level principles that many moral traditions can accept even when they disagree about ultimate foundations: respect for autonomy, nonmaleficence, beneficence and justice.

Respect for autonomy means respecting the capacity of a person with decision-making ability to hold views, make choices and act on them. In practice it generates duties of truthful disclosure, informed consent, confidentiality and respect for refusal. Nonmaleficence is the duty not to inflict harm, and beneficence is the duty to contribute to welfare, which includes preventing and removing harm. The two are separated because they behave differently: the duty not to harm is generally stronger and more stringent than the duty to benefit. Justice concerns fair distribution of benefits, risks and costs, and is usually divided into distributive justice, procedural fairness and rights-based claims.

The key logical feature is that the principles are prima facie binding. A prima facie duty is binding unless it conflicts with an equal or stronger duty in the circumstances. No principle is lexically ranked above the others. When they conflict, the method is specification and balancing: specify what the principle means in context, then weigh the competing considerations with explicit reasons that could be defended to others. Beauchamp and Childress also describe the justification of the underlying norms through the common morality and reflective equilibrium, which means adjusting principles and judgments about cases against each other until they cohere.

Principlism has well-known critiques. Critics say it is a checklist that does not tell you what to do when principles collide, that it is distinctively American in its priority on autonomy, and that it lacks a unifying theory. Defenders reply that a pluralist framework is more honest about moral life than one master theory. A good student can both use the four principles and say where they run out.

Worked example. A competent 70-year-old with an operable but risky tumour refuses surgery that her surgeon thinks would probably cure her. Beneficence and nonmaleficence are in tension, since surgery offers benefit and risks harm, but autonomy is decisive about whether to accept the risk of an intervention on her own body, provided she has capacity and understands. The clinician's task is to explore her reasons, correct misunderstandings, and offer alternatives; if capacity and understanding are intact, her informed refusal governs. Justice may enter later if her choice affects scarce resources, but it does not override a competent refusal here.

A common trap is to treat autonomy as a trump card. In the framework it is one principle among four, and its weight depends on whether the choice is truly autonomous and what harm to others is at stake.

lessons.title: Virtue Ethics, Deontology and Consequentialism
body: Principlism is a mid-level toolkit. Underneath it sit the great families of moral theory, and a medical ethicist should be able to say what each one adds and where each struggles.

Consequentialism holds that an act is right to the extent that it produces the best outcomes. Its classical form, utilitarianism, counts the welfare of everyone affected impartially. In medicine it underlies much public health reasoning, cost-effectiveness analysis and triage: when resources are limited, choose the policy that does the most good overall. Its standard objection is that it can seem to license sacrificing an individual for aggregate benefit, as when a healthy person is imagined as an organ source for five patients. Sophisticated consequentialists reply that rules protecting individuals, such as consent, tend to produce better results in the long run.

Deontology, associated with Immanuel Kant, holds that some duties bind regardless of outcomes. A central formulation is that persons must be treated as ends in themselves and never merely as means. This grounds respect for consent, bans on deceptive experimentation, and the idea that a patient has rights that cannot be traded off for utility. Its difficulty is how to resolve conflicts between duties, and the charge that rigid rules can produce bad outcomes, such as a truth-telling rule that seems to demand cruelty.

Virtue ethics, traced to Aristotle, shifts the question from what should I do to what kind of person should I be. The focus is on character traits such as compassion, practical wisdom (phronesis), integrity, courage and trustworthiness. It fits the professional tradition, where the good doctor is described by dispositions as well as rules, and it explains why two clinicians can follow the same rules and yet differ in how they treat patients. Its weakness is action guidance: advice to do what the virtuous person would do is hard to apply in a novel dilemma.

The doctrine of double effect is a bridging idea from the deontological tradition. It says that an action with both a good and a bad effect can be permissible if the action itself is not wrong, the bad effect is foreseen but not intended as a means to the good, the good effect is not produced by way of the bad, and the good outweighs the bad. It is used to analyse, for example, giving opioids to relieve dying patients' suffering with a foreseen risk of hastening death.

Worked example. A hospital must decide whether to adopt a policy that shortens waiting lists by reducing consent discussion time. A consequentialist asks about total outcomes, a deontologist asks whether the policy treats patients as mere means, and a virtue theorist asks what the policy does to clinicians' attentiveness and patients' trust. Each lens flags something the others can miss.

lessons.title: Care Ethics, Narrative Medicine and Casuistry
body: Not every ethical approach begins with a principle or a theory. Three influential alternatives begin from relationships, stories and cases.

Care ethics emerged from feminist philosophy in the 1980s, associated with Carol Gilligan, whose book In a Different Voice challenged models of moral development that treated abstract justice reasoning as the highest form, and with Nel Noddings and Joan Tronto. It holds that moral life is built from relationships of dependence and responsiveness, and that attentiveness, responsibility, competence and responsiveness to the cared-for person are central moral activities. In medicine it draws attention to vulnerability, to the unpaid caregiving that sustains health systems, and to how power differences shape a clinical encounter. Its critics worry that it can slide into paternalism or parochialism, favouring those close to us. Its defenders say it corrects an overly individualist picture of the patient as a free-standing chooser.

Narrative medicine, developed by Rita Charon, treats clinical practice as an encounter with stories. Patients present illness as a narrative that has a before, a meaning and a future, and clinicians need narrative competence: the ability to absorb, interpret and respond to stories. Close reading of literature and reflective writing are used to train this skill. The ethical point is that a diagnosis is not the whole truth about a person. A treatment decision that is correct on the numbers may still fail if it ignores what the illness means in the patient's life. The method has been criticised for resting on thin empirical evidence about whether it improves care, so its claims are best presented as a plausible and widely adopted approach rather than a proven intervention.

Casuistry is case-based reasoning. Albert Jonsen and Stephen Toulmin, in The Abuse of Casuistry (1988), revived an older tradition of reasoning from paradigm cases, where agreement exists about a clear instance, to harder cases by analogy and by attention to circumstances. This mirrors how common-law courts work, and it matches how experienced ethics consultants often reason. Jonsen's four-topics method, using medical indications, patient preferences, quality of life and contextual features, is a practical form of it. Its weakness is that analogies can be chosen to fit a desired answer, so someone must still justify which cases count as paradigms.
These approaches are best seen as complements. A principle names what is at stake, a narrative shows whose life it is, and a case shows how similar problems have been resolved.

Worked example. An elderly woman with advanced heart failure declines a defibrillator. The principlist sees autonomy and nonmaleficence. The narrative reader hears that her husband died after a long intensive-care stay and that she fears the same ending. The care ethicist notes that her daughter, who provides daily care, was not consulted. The casuist compares her case to paradigm refusals of life-prolonging treatment. A good consultation draws on all four.

lessons.title: The Hippocratic Tradition and the Modern Codes
body: The Hippocratic Oath is a short Greek text from the classical period, traditionally attributed to the Hippocratic school of around the fifth to fourth century BCE, though its authorship is unknown. It binds the physician to teachers and students, to benefit patients according to ability and judgment, to refuse to give a deadly drug or to administer an abortifacient pessary in the original text, to keep patients' secrets, and to avoid sexual exploitation of those in the household. The popular phrase first do no harm does not appear in the Oath. A related idea, to help or at least to do no harm, appears in the Hippocratic Epidemics, and the Latin tag primum non nocere is of later origin. The Oath's lasting influence is the idea of medicine as a profession with duties to patients, but it is also strongly paternalistic: the physician decides what benefits the patient.

Later landmarks include Thomas Percival's Medical Ethics (1803), which codified etiquette and duties in the English-speaking world, and the American Medical Association's first Code of Ethics (1847), which drew on Percival. The twentieth century added codes responding to catastrophe.

The Nuremberg Code (1947) came from the judgment in the Doctors' Trial, in which American military judges tried Nazi physicians for crimes including coercive experiments on concentration camp prisoners. Its first principle states that the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential, and it sets out conditions such as a scientific rationale, avoidance of unnecessary suffering, and the subject's right to withdraw. It was not a law of any country and it was criticised as too absolute, especially for research on children and incapacitated persons.

The Declaration of Helsinki, issued by the World Medical Association in 1964 and revised many times since, is the principal international statement on research ethics. It differs from Nuremberg by recognising the role of independent ethics committee review, accepting surrogate consent for those who cannot consent, and distinguishing clinical research from therapy. The Declaration of Geneva (1948) is a modernised physician's pledge and a separate document.

The Belmont Report (1979) was produced by the US National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects, established under the National Research Act of 1974 after the Tuskegee revelations. It identified three principles: respect for persons, beneficence and justice, and tied them to informed consent, risk-benefit assessment and fair selection of subjects. Belmont's principles fed into the US federal regulations on human subjects research, the Common Rule (45 CFR 46), and influenced principlism.

Worked example. A research proposal would give a placebo to children with a treatable condition. Nuremberg does not directly address it, Helsinki requires independent review and justification, and Belmont tells reviewers to ask whether risks are justified and whether the burden falls fairly. Knowing which document says what is a common exam trap.

lessons.title: Informed Consent: Elements, Standards and Exceptions
body: Informed consent is both an ethical doctrine and a legal one. Ethically it expresses respect for autonomy: a person's body and life are theirs to direct. Legally it is the reason a touching that would otherwise be a battery is lawful, and it is the basis of a negligence claim when a clinician fails to disclose material information.

The standard ethical elements are: threshold elements (capacity and voluntariness), information elements (disclosure of material information, a recommendation, and understanding of both), and consent elements (a decision in favour of a plan and authorisation of it). Voluntariness means freedom from coercion and from controlling manipulation, though persuasion by honest argument is allowed. The information that must be disclosed typically includes the nature of the proposed intervention, its risks and expected benefits, reasonable alternatives including no treatment, and the consequences of declining.

The history shows the doctrine's shape. In Schloendorff v. Society of New York Hospital (New York, 1914), Judge Cardozo recognised that an adult of sound mind has the right to decide what is done with his body, and that surgery without consent is a battery. The phrase informed consent entered American law in Salgo v. Leland Stanford Jr. University Board of Trustees (California Court of Appeal, 1957), which required disclosure of facts necessary to form an intelligent consent. Canterbury v. Spence (D.C. Circuit, 1972) shifted the measure of disclosure.

States divide on the standard of disclosure. Under the professional (reasonable physician) standard, the physician must disclose what a reasonable physician in the same community or specialty would disclose. Under the patient-oriented (reasonable patient) standard, adopted in Canterbury, the physician must disclose what a reasonable person in the patient's position would consider material to the decision. Jurisdictions are split, and neither is simply the majority rule across the whole country. A claim based on nondisclosure is usually brought in negligence and requires causation: the plaintiff must show that a reasonable person in her position would not have consented had the risk been disclosed, and that the undisclosed risk materialised. A battery claim is reserved, in most states, for treatment that differs fundamentally from what was consented to.

There are recognised exceptions. In a true emergency where the patient lacks capacity and no surrogate is available, consent is implied for necessary lifesaving care. Patients may waive disclosure, though the waiver must itself be informed and voluntary. Therapeutic privilege, withholding information because disclosure itself would harm the patient, is very narrow and cannot be used merely because the patient might refuse. Treatment under legal compulsion, for example some public health orders, is a separate category with its own procedural safeguards.

Worked example. A surgeon fails to mention a known 1 percent risk of nerve injury that a reasonable patient would consider material. The patient has the operation, the injury occurs, and the surgeon performed it competently. The surgery itself was not negligent, but under a reasonable-patient jurisdiction the nondisclosure may be actionable if the patient proves she would have declined the procedure had she known. Under a physician standard, the answer would depend on what comparable surgeons disclose.

lessons.title: Decision-Making Capacity
body: Capacity is a patient's ability to make a particular healthcare decision. It is a threshold for informed consent: a person who lacks it cannot give or refuse valid consent, and decisions then pass to a surrogate or to a best-interests process. Three features make capacity easy to mishandle, so a student should be able to state them clearly.

First, capacity is decision-specific. A patient may have capacity to choose a simple treatment and lack it for a complex one, or have it at one time of day and lack it at another because of delirium or sedation. It is not an on-off property of the person. Second, the more serious the consequences of a decision, the more carefully capacity should be examined, which is sometimes described as a sliding scale. A sliding scale does not mean that disagreement with the clinician is evidence of incapacity. Third, capacity is a clinical judgment made by the treating clinician, while competence is a legal status determined by a court. In practice the words are often used loosely, but a court adjudicates competence and appoints a guardian where needed.

The widely used framework from Appelbaum and Grisso identifies four abilities. Understanding: can the patient grasp the relevant information about condition, options and consequences? Appreciation: can the patient recognise that the information applies to him, rather than acknowledging facts in the abstract? Reasoning: can the patient manipulate information rationally and weigh options against his own values? Expressing a choice: can the patient communicate a stable decision? Appreciation is where psychiatric conditions often interfere, for example when a patient with severe depression accepts that treatment works for others but believes he is beyond help, or a patient with delusions denies that he is ill.

Important traps follow. A refusal of recommended treatment, a bad decision, or an unusual religious belief does not by itself show lack of capacity. A psychiatric diagnosis or an intellectual disability does not equal incapacity. Conversely, a patient who agrees with the clinician may still lack capacity, and assent from such a patient should not be treated as consent. Reversible causes such as infection, pain, hypoglycaemia, or medication effects should be sought and treated, and the assessment repeated.

In England and Wales the Mental Capacity Act 2005 sets out a statutory test and begins from a presumption of capacity; in the United States there is no single federal capacity test, and the standard is set by state law and common practice. If a patient lacks capacity, the clinician follows a prior valid directive where there is one, otherwise a surrogate, and if there is a dispute or no surrogate an ethics consultation or court may be needed.

Worked example. A 66-year-old man with confusion from a urinary infection refuses antibiotics, saying that he is fine and that the staff are poisoning him. He can repeat the risks but insists he has no infection. He fails appreciation and reasoning, so he lacks capacity for this decision at this time. The team treats the delirium and re-assesses, rather than labelling him permanently incompetent.

lessons.title: Confidentiality and Its Limits
body: Confidentiality is among the oldest duties in medicine, appearing in the Hippocratic Oath. Its justification is partly consequentialist and partly rights-based. Patients who fear disclosure may withhold facts or avoid care, which harms them and public health, and a person's health information is part of a private sphere that deserves respect in its own right. The duty is strong but not absolute, and a clear account of where it yields is a core professional skill.

In the United States the main federal source is the HIPAA Privacy Rule (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164), issued under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996. It applies to covered entities (most health care providers, health plans and clearinghouses) and their business associates. Protected health information may be used and disclosed without individual authorisation for treatment, payment and health care operations, so sharing a chart with a consulting specialist needs no signed release. Other uses generally need written authorisation. The Rule also permits or requires disclosure in specified situations, including some public health activities, reporting of abuse and neglect, certain law enforcement and judicial purposes, and to avert a serious and imminent threat to health or safety. Disclosures are generally limited to the minimum necessary, except for treatment. State law may be more protective, and records of substance use disorder treatment from federally assisted programmes have a separate regulation (42 CFR Part 2). HIPAA is a regulatory scheme, not itself a private right to sue, though state tort and professional discipline may apply.

Common ethical grounds for breaching confidentiality are a serious risk to an identifiable third party, mandatory reporting laws (for example child abuse in all states, and in many places certain infectious diseases and some injuries), and a court order. The classic case is Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California (California Supreme Court, 1976), where a patient told his psychologist he intended to kill a woman and then did. The court held that when a therapist determines, or under professional standards should determine, that a patient poses a serious danger of violence to another, the therapist must use reasonable care to protect the intended victim. That may include warning the victim or others, notifying police, or taking other reasonable steps. States have responded differently: some impose a mandatory duty to warn or protect, some make disclosure permissive, and some decline to recognise a duty. A student must therefore name the split rather than treat Tarasoff as a nationwide rule.

Particular traps include minors, where state law determines which services a minor may consent to and therefore who controls the information, and family members, who have no automatic right to information unless the patient agrees or the law provides. Verbal discussion with a family member present at the bedside with the patient's apparent agreement is usually acceptable.

Worked example. A patient with newly diagnosed HIV declines to tell his wife. The physician urges him to do so and offers help. Where state law and professional guidance allow disclosure to an identifiable person at significant risk, and the patient persistently refuses, the clinician checks the jurisdiction's rules and often involves the public health department's partner-notification services rather than disclosing unilaterally. The mere fact of risk to a spouse does not by itself dissolve confidentiality everywhere.

lessons.title: Truth-Telling and Disclosure of Bad News
body: Until the later twentieth century, concealing a serious diagnosis from the patient was common practice in many countries. A frequently cited American survey from 1961 found that most physicians said they usually avoided telling patients that they had cancer, and later surveys found the practice had reversed. The shift followed the rise of patient autonomy, effective treatments that made disclosure less hopeless, and the legal development of informed consent. Today the dominant norm in American and European medicine is truthful disclosure, but the reasoning behind it remains worth knowing.

The ethical arguments for truth-telling are several. Autonomy needs information, so a patient who is deceived cannot decide for herself. Deception breaches the trust on which the clinical relationship depends. Kant argued that lying is wrong in itself, while consequentialists point to long-term loss of trust in medicine. Arguments against full disclosure rest mainly on beneficence: bad news may cause distress, destroy hope, or worsen outcomes. Evidence that most patients wish to be told, and that honest communication does not generally cause the harms feared, has weakened this argument in most settings. It remains true that patients differ in how much they want to know, and that clinicians should find out.

Several refinements matter. Truth-telling is not the same as unloading all information at once; disclosure can be paced, begun by asking what the patient already understands and how much they want to know. The right not to know is recognised: a patient may decline details, for example genetic risk information, and the clinician should respect this while ensuring the patient knows what is available. Therapeutic privilege, withholding information on the ground that disclosure would seriously harm the patient, is legally narrow and ethically controversial, and it is not available simply because the clinician thinks the patient would refuse. Cultural and family practices vary; some patients prefer that a relative receive information first. The best response is to ask the patient how they want information shared, not to assume either way. Requests by relatives to hide a diagnosis from a capable patient should not be followed as such, but they are a signal to explore the family's fears and the patient's wishes.

The SPIKES protocol (Baile and colleagues, 2000) is a widely taught six-step approach to delivering bad news: Setting up, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, and Strategy and Summary. It is a communication aid, not an ethical theory.

Placebo use raises a related issue. Prescribing an inert substance while telling the patient it is an active drug is deception and sits badly with informed consent, while open-label placebo is a separate research topic. Honesty also applies to prognosis: clinicians tend to overestimate survival, and patients are poorly served by vague reassurance.

Worked example. The daughter of an 80-year-old woman with newly found pancreatic cancer asks the doctor to tell her mother only that she has a growth. The doctor meets the daughter, explains that the mother has a right to information, and asks what worries her. Then, with the mother, the doctor asks how much she wishes to know and offers to share as much or as little as she prefers. If the mother asks directly, she is told the truth.

lessons.title: Surrogate Decision-Making and Advance Care Planning
body: When a patient lacks capacity, someone else must decide. The ethical aim is to respect the patient as far as possible, and three standards guide the surrogate in descending order of preference.

The first is the expressed wish: if the patient left a valid advance directive or clearly stated instructions that apply to the situation, they are followed. The second is substituted judgment: the surrogate asks what this particular patient would choose if she could see her situation, drawing on her values and past statements. The third is the best interests standard: if nothing is known about the patient's wishes, the surrogate and clinicians choose what a reasonable person would see as most beneficial, weighing benefits and burdens. The surrogate is not asked what the surrogate would want for himself, and a common error is to substitute the family's preferences for the patient's.

Who is the surrogate? Most US states have statutes setting a default hierarchy for those without a designated agent, commonly beginning with a court-appointed guardian, then the spouse or partner, adult children, parents and siblings, though the order and the inclusion of unmarried partners and close friends vary by state. A patient can avoid default rules by appointing a health care agent through a durable power of attorney for health care, sometimes called a health care proxy.

Advance directives take two main forms. A living will states preferences about treatments in particular circumstances, such as refusal of ventilation if terminally ill. A durable power of attorney for health care appoints an agent to decide. Each has weaknesses: a living will cannot anticipate every situation and its wording can be vague, while an agent may be unsure what the patient would want, so the best practice combines them and records the conversation. POLST (Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment, with state variants in name and form) is a different instrument: a portable medical order for seriously ill or frail patients, signed by a clinician after a conversation, not a directive for healthy people. A do-not-resuscitate order is a specific order to forgo cardiopulmonary resuscitation. The Patient Self-Determination Act of 1990 requires hospitals and other institutions receiving Medicare or Medicaid funds to inform patients about their right to make directives.

Two landmark cases frame the law. In re Quinlan (New Jersey Supreme Court, 1976) allowed the father of a young woman in a persistent vegetative state to authorise removal of her ventilator, relying on privacy rights and the family's role. Cruzan v. Director, Missouri Department of Health (US Supreme Court, 1990) assumed that a competent person has a constitutionally protected liberty interest in refusing unwanted treatment, including artificial nutrition and hydration, but held that a state may require clear and convincing evidence of an incompetent patient's wishes before a surrogate may withdraw treatment. Cruzan therefore tells us a state may demand a high evidentiary standard, not that every state must.

Worked example. A 75-year-old man with advanced dementia develops pneumonia. His daughter says she cannot bear to lose him and wants everything done. The team asks her what he would say. She recalls that he often said he never wanted to live "hooked to machines". The surrogate's task is to report his values, not her own preference, and the team supports her through that reframing, which is substituted judgment applied.

lessons.title: Palliative Care and Withdrawing Treatment
body: Palliative care is specialised care for people living with serious illness, aimed at relieving symptoms and suffering and supporting patients and families, at any stage and alongside disease-directed treatment. The World Health Organization defines it as an approach that improves quality of life by prevention and relief of suffering through early identification and treatment of pain and other problems. Hospice is a model of palliative care for people near the end of life. In the United States the Medicare hospice benefit is available when a physician certifies that the patient would likely die within six months if the illness runs its expected course, and it continues if the patient lives longer and is recertified. Palliative care itself does not require a terminal prognosis, and a patient is not abandoning treatment by accepting it.

A basic ethical and legal principle is that withholding and withdrawing life-sustaining treatment are morally equivalent when the treatment is not wanted or no longer serves the patient's goals. If a ventilator trial is started and the patient does not recover, stopping it is not killing; the underlying disease causes death. The mistaken view that withdrawing is worse than never starting leads clinicians to avoid starting treatments that might help, for fear of being unable to stop. A patient has the right to refuse any treatment, and the law, as in Cruzan, generally treats artificial nutrition and hydration as medical treatment that may be refused or withdrawn like any other. There is no obligation to provide treatments that are medically futile in the sense of offering no physiological benefit, though disputes over what counts as futile or potentially inappropriate are common, and institutions use processes rather than individual vetoes.

The doctrine of double effect applies to symptom control. Opioids and sedatives given to relieve severe suffering in the dying are permissible when the intention is relief, the dose is proportionate to the symptom, and the foreseen risk of hastening death is accepted but not intended. Evidence suggests that appropriately titrated opioids do not generally shorten life, so the risk is often overstated. Palliative sedation, giving sedatives to lower consciousness in a patient with refractory suffering near death, is distinguished from euthanasia by its goal, the proportionality of the drug and the underlying cause of death, though critics argue that the line is thinner in practice. Voluntarily stopping eating and drinking is a recognised path in which a capable patient declines oral intake, and it is legally treated as a refusal of treatment rather than assisted suicide in most jurisdictions.

Death can be determined by neurological criteria, often called brain death, under the Uniform Determination of Death Act (1981), which most states have adopted. That is a different question from withdrawing treatment from a living patient. Some states provide accommodation for religious objections.

Worked example. A 68-year-old with end-stage lung disease on ventilator support after a failed trial of therapy has no realistic chance of leaving intensive care. His surrogate, applying his earlier statements, asks to stop the ventilator. The team provides opioids and sedatives to control breathlessness and distress as the ventilator is withdrawn. Withdrawal is not euthanasia, and the symptom medication is justified by double effect and proportionality.

lessons.title: Assisted Dying: The Positions and the Law
body: Terms matter. Euthanasia is a clinician deliberately ending a patient's life, usually by injecting a lethal drug, at the patient's request (voluntary), without it (non-voluntary, where the patient cannot consent) or against the patient's wishes (involuntary, which is murder everywhere). Physician-assisted suicide, also called physician-assisted dying or aid in dying, means the physician provides a means, usually a prescription for a lethal dose, that the patient takes. In some places both are grouped as medical assistance in dying. All of these differ from refusing or withdrawing treatment and from palliative care, discussed in the previous lesson, which are lawful in principle everywhere in the United States.

The main arguments in favour rest on autonomy and compassion. A capable adult facing unrelievable suffering, it is said, has a right to decide the manner and time of her death, and a clinician who helps acts out of mercy. Defenders add that the distinction between withdrawing treatment and assisting death is thin, since both foreseeably end life at a patient's request. The main arguments against rest on the intrinsic value of life, the integrity of the medical profession, and risks of abuse. Opponents argue that the doctor's role is to heal and comfort, and not to kill, that safeguards may erode over time (the slippery slope claim, whose empirical support is itself disputed), that disabled, poor or elderly people may feel pressure to choose death, that prognoses are uncertain, and that better palliative care should address suffering. Both sides are serious. Evidence about slippery slopes comes mostly from Oregon, the Netherlands and Belgium, and people interpret it differently. Professional bodies are divided: the American Medical Association's Code of Medical Ethics opposes physician-assisted suicide, while some groups take a position of studied neutrality or support.

Law, as of this writing, varies sharply. In the United States, the Supreme Court held in Washington v. Glucksberg (1997) that there is no constitutional right to assistance in suicide, and in Vacco v. Quill (1997) that a state may distinguish between refusing life-sustaining treatment and assisted suicide without violating equal protection. These decisions left the question to the states. Oregon's Death with Dignity Act (adopted by ballot in 1994, in effect from 1997) was the first statute, and a number of other jurisdictions have since authorised physician-assisted dying, including Washington, Vermont, California, Colorado, Hawaii, New Jersey, Maine, New Mexico, the District of Columbia, Delaware (in effect 1 January 2026), New York (in effect 5 August 2026) and Illinois (in effect 12 September 2026), and in Montana a state supreme court decision, Baxter v. Montana (2009), allows it as a defence. Treat this as a snapshot as of October 2026: the list has been growing, so check current status. Typical statutes limit access to adults with decision-making capacity, a terminal illness with a prognosis of six months or less, and a request to self-administer an oral medication, with two physicians and waiting periods. Euthanasia is not lawful in any US state.

Elsewhere, the Netherlands and Belgium (both 2002) permit euthanasia and assisted suicide under due-care criteria, Canada permits medical assistance in dying following Carter v. Canada (2015) and legislation in 2016, later broadened, and Switzerland does not criminalise assisting suicide when it is not done for selfish motives. Spain and New Zealand (both 2021) have adopted laws, and as of August 2026 every Australian state and territory has legislated for voluntary assisted dying, though the Northern Territory scheme is not yet operating. Assisting suicide remains a crime in England and Wales under the Suicide Act 1961. A Commons-passed bill to change that fell when the parliamentary session ended in April 2026, and a reintroduced bill was defeated at second reading on 11 September 2026 by 286 votes to 270, so the law is unchanged, though the debate continues.

Worked example. A student asked to evaluate a law requiring a six-month prognosis should separate three questions: whether prognosis can be predicted accurately, whether suffering is only a feature of terminal illness, and whether a safeguard exists for decision-making capacity. The first and third are empirical and procedural, the second is a value judgment. Separating them is more useful than choosing sides.

lessons.title: Reproductive Ethics: Contraception, Abortion, Assisted Reproduction and Prenatal Testing
body: Reproductive ethics touches some of the deepest disagreements in medicine. The task here is not to resolve them but to be able to state the strongest versions of each position, to identify the factual and the evaluative questions, and to state the current law accurately.

Abortion. The central ethical question is the moral status of the embryo or fetus and how it weighs against the pregnant woman's interests and rights. One family of positions holds that the fetus has the full moral status of a person from conception, or from a very early point, so abortion is wrong except perhaps to save the woman's life. Another holds that moral status develops gradually, for example with sentience or viability, so early abortion is permissible and later abortion needs stronger reasons. A third argues, following Judith Jarvis Thomson, that even if the fetus is a person, bodily autonomy means a woman is not obligated to continue a pregnancy, and critics reply that the analogy fails because of the special relation of parent to child and the difference between killing and letting die. A fourth stresses justice: restrictions fall most heavily on poor women and affect health outcomes. Each can be given in its strongest form without strawmen. Public views are divided, and many people hold mixed positions that depend on stage and circumstance.

Law. In Roe v. Wade (1973) and Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992), the Supreme Court recognised a constitutional right to abortion before viability. In Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022), the Court overruled both, holding that the Constitution does not confer a right to abortion and that regulation returns to the people and their elected representatives. As of this writing, abortion law is set mostly by states and varies widely, from broad legal access to near-total bans with narrow exceptions, and the details change frequently through legislation and litigation. Students should therefore check current state law and not assume a national rule. Federal law also contains conscientious objection protections for some providers, such as the Church Amendments.

Contraception and sterilisation raise issues of autonomy, coercion and history, including eugenic sterilisation programmes in the early twentieth century, one of which was upheld in Buck v. Bell (1927), a decision widely condemned today. Informed choice and avoidance of coercion are the central principles.

Assisted reproduction raises questions about the moral status of embryos, disposition of frozen embryos, donor anonymity and the child's interest in knowing origins, commercial surrogacy (legal in some jurisdictions and prohibited in others), and fair access given costs. Preimplantation genetic testing and prenatal screening raise a debated expressivist objection: that selecting against disability may express a negative view of disabled lives, whereas defenders argue that choices are about the situation of a particular family, not a judgment of worth.

Maternal-fetal conflict arises when a pregnant woman declines recommended treatment. Courts in the United States have, with few exceptions, held that a competent pregnant patient keeps the right to refuse, and professional bodies such as the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists advise against coercion.

Worked example. A clinician asked about an abortion request does not first ask whether it is right. She asks whether the patient has capacity, is free of coercion, understands the options, and what state law requires, and she follows a conscientious objection policy that ensures timely referral if she declines to participate.

lessons.title: Historical Abuses in Research and What They Taught
body: Research ethics rules were built in response to specific, documented abuses. Learning them accurately matters, because the lessons are only as good as the facts.

The Nazi medical experiments, including freezing, high-altitude, infectious disease and sterilisation experiments on prisoners in concentration camps, led to the Doctors' Trial at Nuremberg (1946 to 1947) and the Nuremberg Code. The judgment's response was to state that the voluntary consent of the subject is essential.

The Tuskegee study is the best-known American case. From 1932 until 1972 the US Public Health Service followed about 600 Black men in Macon County, Alabama, around 400 of whom had syphilis and about 200 of whom did not, to observe the natural history of untreated disease. The men were told they were being treated for bad blood and were not told they had syphilis or that they were research subjects in a study of untreated disease. When penicillin became the standard cure in the 1940s, it was not offered to them, and efforts were made to keep them from receiving treatment elsewhere. The study ended in 1972 after Peter Buxtun, a Public Health Service employee, raised concerns and the story was reported in the press. A class action settlement followed, and President Clinton formally apologised in 1997. The study is often misdescribed as one in which researchers infected the men with syphilis. That is false: the men already had the disease, and the wrong was in withholding information and effective treatment and in deceiving them. It also left an enduring legacy of distrust in some Black communities, which research on vaccine and clinical trial participation has examined.

Other cases show the pattern. The Willowbrook State School studies (1956 onward) deliberately infected children with intellectual disabilities with hepatitis to study the disease and a possible vaccine; parental consent was obtained but was criticised as coerced, since admission to the overcrowded institution was in some reports linked to enrolment. In 1963 the Jewish Chronic Disease Hospital study injected live cancer cells into elderly patients without telling them what they were. Henry Beecher's 1966 article in the New England Journal of Medicine catalogued 22 examples of ethically troubling research at respected US institutions. The US Public Health Service also conducted syphilis experiments in Guatemala between 1946 and 1948, in which prisoners, soldiers and psychiatric patients were deliberately exposed to infection, and a US presidential commission examined it in 2011. The case of Henrietta Lacks, whose cervical cancer cells were taken in 1951 and became the HeLa line without her knowledge, is generally treated as a consent and ownership issue, not an experiment on a person, and it influenced debates about the use of tissues.

The regulatory response in the United States was the National Research Act of 1974, which required institutional review boards for federally funded research and created the commission that wrote the Belmont Report. Federal rules for human subjects research are now codified in 45 CFR 46, the Common Rule. In 1999, the death of Jesse Gelsinger, an 18-year-old in a gene therapy trial at the University of Pennsylvania, brought attention to the adequacy of consent and to investigators' financial interests.

Worked example. A student asked what Tuskegee shows should avoid the myth that researchers gave the men syphilis, and should explain that the abuse was deception and denial of an available cure, which led directly to informed consent and independent review as requirements.

lessons.title: Research Ethics Today: Review, Consent, Equipoise and Vulnerable Subjects
body: Research differs from treatment in its primary aim. Clinical care aims at the patient's benefit, while research aims at generalisable knowledge, with the participant's benefit incidental. That difference means the clinician's duties of beneficence cannot be assumed to cover the researcher's role, and extra safeguards apply.

Oversight in the United States centres on the institutional review board (IRB), a committee that reviews proposed research under the Common Rule (45 CFR 46) and, for drug and device trials, Food and Drug Administration regulations. Criteria for approval include minimising risks, reasonable risks in relation to anticipated benefits and the importance of the knowledge, equitable selection of subjects, informed consent that is sought and documented, and provisions for data monitoring and confidentiality. Internationally, ethics committees fulfil a similar function under the Declaration of Helsinki and the CIOMS guidelines. Large trials usually have an independent data and safety monitoring board that can stop a study early for harm, clear benefit or futility.

Consent in research is more demanding than in treatment, because the participant takes risks for others. The consent process must explain the purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, alternatives, confidentiality, that participation is voluntary, and the right to withdraw without penalty. A frequent trap is therapeutic misconception: participants, including intelligent ones, assume that the trial is designed for their personal benefit, for example that random assignment reflects a doctor's choice. Good consent explicitly counters it.

The ethical justification for randomising people between treatments is equipoise. Classical theoretical equipoise means the investigator has no good reason to prefer one arm. Benjamin Freedman's clinical equipoise, proposed in 1987, means genuine uncertainty or disagreement within the expert community about which treatment is better. Without equipoise, assigning participants to what is believed to be an inferior treatment is hard to justify. Placebo controls are acceptable where no proven effective therapy exists or when withholding it poses no risk of serious harm, and they are contested otherwise. A trial may be stopped early because interim data show clear benefit or harm, but stopping rules and interim analyses raise statistical and ethical issues, because early stopping for benefit tends to overestimate effect sizes.

Vulnerable subjects need added protection. The US regulations contain subparts for pregnant women, prisoners and children. Research with children generally requires parental permission plus the child's assent where appropriate, and risk above minimal needs a prospect of direct benefit or a narrow, important justification. Adults who lack capacity may enrol through a legally authorised representative. The ethical aim is neither blanket exclusion, which deprives these groups of evidence-based care, nor unprotected inclusion.

Other topics include conflicts of interest of investigators, post-trial access to beneficial interventions in trials run in low-income countries, and the controversy surrounding trials in which a control group in a poorer country was given a less effective regimen than the standard elsewhere, as in disputes about the 1990s perinatal HIV transmission trials. Research integrity, including fabrication, falsification and plagiarism, is a separate matter.

Worked example. A trial plans to randomise patients with an untreated but serious infection to a new drug or placebo, despite an established effective antibiotic. An IRB would ask whether withholding the antibiotic poses serious risk, since if so the placebo arm cannot be justified and the control should be active treatment.

lessons.title: Resource Allocation and Distributive Justice
body: Scarcity is a fact of health care. Organs, intensive care beds, specialist time and budgets are limited, so someone must decide who gets what, whether openly or implicitly. Allocation ethics asks which reasons for those decisions are legitimate.

The main distributive theories each pick out something that matters. Utilitarian or maximising approaches aim to produce the greatest total benefit, for example the most lives or the most life-years saved, often measured in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), which combine length and quality of life. Egalitarian approaches stress equal worth and favour giving everyone an equal chance, for instance by lottery among similar claimants, or equal access to a decent minimum of care. Prioritarian views give extra weight to benefits for the worst off, which in medicine usually means the sickest or those who would otherwise lose the most. Libertarian approaches emphasise voluntary exchange and property rights and are sceptical of claims on others' resources. John Rawls's theory of justice as fairness and Norman Daniels's extension of it to health argue that health care protects a fair equality of opportunity and is therefore of special moral importance. Many real systems blend these views.

Tension is easy to see. Saving the most lives may favour treating those with the best prognosis, while a prioritarian would favour the sickest. Maximising life-years favours the young, which some regard as fair under a life-cycle or fair innings argument that everyone should have a chance at a normal span, while others see it as age discrimination. QALYs are criticised as discriminating against people with chronic illness or disability, because their quality-of-life weights are lower, and some legal systems and professional guidance therefore avoid them. In England the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence uses a threshold, of 25 to 35 thousand pounds per QALY since April 2026 (raised from 20 to 30 thousand, the range used for about two decades), in appraising technologies, though that is a decision rule and not a fixed law of nature.

Organ allocation shows a constructed system. In the United States, the National Organ Transplant Act of 1984 prohibits buying and selling organs and created the national transplant network, run under federal contract and known as the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network. Allocation policies use factors such as medical urgency, expected benefit, blood and tissue matching, waiting time and geography, and explicitly exclude social worth, wealth and celebrity. Debates focus on whether geography should determine access and how to weigh urgency against likely benefit.

During surges such as the COVID-19 pandemic, hospitals developed crisis standards of care, with triage protocols that used measures of short-term survival, such as the SOFA score, and sometimes a lottery for ties. The best protocols were developed before the crisis, applied by triage teams separate from the treating clinician, and open to appeal. Daniels and Sabin's accountability for reasonableness gives a framework for legitimate decisions where people disagree on principles: publicity of the reasons, relevance of the reasons, a process of appeal and revision, and enforcement. Disability-rights law, including the Americans with Disabilities Act, forbids categorical exclusion of people because of disability, so the focus is on individualised assessment of likelihood of benefit.

Worked example. Two ventilators are available and three patients need them: a healthy 30-year-old nurse, a 72-year-old with moderate prognosis, and a 40-year-old with a poor prognosis. A utilitarian triage ranks by likelihood of survival, so the nurse and the 72-year-old may receive them. A lottery among equals would apply only if prognoses are equal. Using the patient's social status or ability to pay would be inconsistent with every mainstream theory.

lessons.title: Conflicts of Interest in Medicine
body: A conflict of interest exists when a professional's secondary interest, such as financial gain, career advancement or a relationship, creates a risk of undue influence on judgment concerning a primary interest, such as patient welfare or the integrity of research. The conflict is the risk, not an accusation of misconduct. A clinician can be conflicted without being corrupt, and a conflict can distort judgment without the person noticing, which is why conflicts are managed by rules and not left to individual conscience.

Examples include industry payments to prescribers for speaking, consulting or meals, ownership of a laboratory or imaging centre to which a physician refers patients, financial stakes in a product that an investigator is testing, authorship of guidelines by experts with industry ties, and pay structures that reward volume. Evidence indicates that even small gifts and interactions are associated with changes in prescribing behaviour, and that industry sponsored trials are more likely to report favourable conclusions than independent ones, as shown in a Cochrane review of the topic, although the mechanisms involve choices of comparator, outcomes and reporting. Most physicians believe they are unaffected, which is itself part of the problem.

Management tools fall along a spectrum: prohibition of the activity, disclosure, and recusal or independent oversight. Disclosure is the most common and the weakest. It informs patients and readers, but it does not remove the conflict, and some experimental work suggests that disclosure can leave recipients no better protected and may even license advisers to be more biased, a result that is debated. Stronger tools include barring conflicted persons from voting on a guideline recommendation or from running a trial, independent data analysis, and institutional policies on gifts.

US law addresses some kinds of conflict. The Physician Payments Sunshine Act, enacted as part of the Affordable Care Act of 2010, requires manufacturers of drugs, devices and supplies covered by federal programmes to report payments and ownership interests to physicians and teaching hospitals, and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services publishes them in a database called Open Payments. The Stark Law prohibits physicians from referring Medicare patients for certain designated health services to entities with which they or their family members have a financial relationship, unless an exception applies. The federal Anti-Kickback Statute makes it a crime to knowingly and willingly offer or accept remuneration to induce referrals of items or services paid by federal health care programmes. Journals require authors to disclose conflicts, and the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors has a standard disclosure form.

Moore v. Regents of the University of California (California Supreme Court, 1990) concerned a patient whose physician used his removed cells to develop a commercially valuable cell line without telling him. The court held that a physician must disclose personal research or economic interests unrelated to the patient's health if they may affect the physician's professional judgment, and that disclosure failure can give rise to claims for breach of fiduciary duty or lack of informed consent. The court declined to find that the patient had a property interest in his cells for a conversion claim.

Worked example. A cardiologist who receives consulting fees from a stent manufacturer is asked to join a hospital committee choosing a stent supplier. The ordinary solution is to disclose the relationship and recuse from the vote, while remaining available to answer technical questions, since disclosure alone leaves the influence on the vote in place.

lessons.title: Medical Error, Disclosure and Patient Safety
body: An adverse event is harm caused by medical care rather than the underlying disease. A medical error is a failure of planned action or use of a wrong plan, and many adverse events involve no error, while some errors cause no harm (near misses). A sentinel event is a patient safety event reaching a patient and causing death, permanent harm or severe temporary harm. A never event is a serious, largely preventable event such as wrong-site surgery or a retained instrument. These distinctions matter because ethics and law treat them differently.

The modern patient safety movement started with the Institute of Medicine report To Err Is Human (1999), which estimated that tens of thousands of Americans die each year from preventable hospital errors. The exact figures are disputed, with later studies producing higher and lower estimates, but the report's lasting contribution was conceptual. It argued that most errors result from faulty systems and processes, not from individual carelessness, so the response should be redesign (checklists, forcing functions, barcode checks, hand-off protocols) rather than only punishment. James Reason's Swiss cheese model describes how harm occurs when holes in several layers of defence line up, so latent conditions such as understaffing and confusing labelling combine with an active failure by a clinician at the sharp end. Root cause analysis and similar methods look for those system contributors.

Just culture is the framework that distinguishes three kinds of behaviour. Human error, a slip or lapse, calls for console and system repair. At-risk behaviour, a drift into shortcuts whose risk is not appreciated, calls for coaching and removing incentives. Reckless behaviour, conscious disregard of a substantial and unjustifiable risk, calls for discipline. The aim is to encourage reporting without excusing recklessness. Punishing every error drives reporting underground.

The ethical duty of disclosure follows from truthfulness, autonomy and trust. A patient who has been harmed by an error needs to know in order to obtain corrective care, make decisions and cope. Professional bodies, including the American Medical Association, the American College of Physicians and the Joint Commission, expect clinicians and institutions to disclose unanticipated outcomes and errors. Good disclosure explains what is known, accepts responsibility where appropriate, expresses regret, describes what will be done to repair and prevent harm, and is followed up. Programmes such as the Communication and Optimal Resolution (CANDOR) toolkit combine prompt disclosure, investigation and early compensation.

Law interacts with this. Many states have enacted apology statutes, which make an expression of sympathy, and in some states an admission of fault, inadmissible as evidence of liability, although their scope varies, so a clinician should know the local law. Some hospitals report that early disclosure with offers of compensation did not raise claims and may have reduced costs, though the evidence base is mixed. Peer review protections in state law shield some internal quality review from discovery, and federal law supports voluntary reporting through the Patient Safety and Quality Improvement Act of 2005. The National Practitioner Data Bank, created under the Health Care Quality Improvement Act of 1986, collects reports of malpractice payments and certain disciplinary actions.

Worked example. A nurse gives a patient ten times the intended dose of insulin through a decimal slip, the error is caught, and the patient is treated in intensive care and recovers. Ethically, the patient should be told what happened and what is being done. The system review asks why the packaging and order screen allowed such an error. Under just culture, the nurse is treated as someone who made a human error in a flawed system, unless an investigation shows reckless behaviour.

lessons.title: Malpractice and the Law of Consent: An Overview
body: Medical malpractice is professional negligence by a health care provider, and a plaintiff must prove the same four elements as in any negligence claim: duty, breach, causation and damages.

Duty arises when a physician-patient relationship exists, usually by agreement to treat. There is generally no duty to treat a stranger, though the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA, 1986) imposes obligations on hospitals with emergency departments that participate in Medicare to screen and stabilise anyone who comes in, regardless of ability to pay. Good Samaritan statutes in states protect certain volunteer rescuers from liability for ordinary negligence.

Breach means falling below the standard of care. The traditional standard asks what a reasonably competent practitioner in the same field would do in similar circumstances. Older law used a locality rule tied to the community, which most jurisdictions have replaced with a national standard, at least for specialists. A specialist is held to the standard of that specialty. The standard of care is nearly always established by expert testimony, since lay jurors cannot judge technical practice. Expert evidence admissibility is governed by Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals (US Supreme Court, 1993) in federal courts and in many states, while other states follow different tests. The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur, the thing speaks for itself, allows an inference of negligence without expert testimony in rare cases where the event does not ordinarily occur without negligence, such as a surgical instrument left inside a patient. Courts apply the doctrine in medicine with some caution. An error of judgment is not negligence if the choice was within the range of acceptable practice, and where a respectable minority of physicians would have taken the same approach, many jurisdictions treat that as acceptable.

Causation has two parts: cause in fact (usually the but-for test, whether harm would have occurred without the breach) and proximate cause. Because patients are often already ill, plaintiffs struggle to prove that negligent delay caused the injury. Loss of chance is now accepted in a majority of states (one 2021 survey counted 29 of 50 as of November 2019, with 15 rejecting it and 6 undecided), allowing recovery when negligence reduced a patient's chance of survival or recovery below fifty percent, while the traditional all-or-nothing rule, still applied in a substantial minority, requires proof that the outcome more likely than not would have differed. Which rule applies depends on the state and may have shifted since, so check current law. Damages include economic losses and non-economic damages such as pain and suffering, and some states cap non-economic damages. Many states impose statutes of limitations running from the injury or its discovery, plus outer limits called statutes of repose.

Consent connects to this framework in two ways. A treatment without any consent, or a procedure substantially different from the one agreed, is traditionally a battery, an intentional tort that does not require proof of negligence. Failure to disclose material risks is treated in most jurisdictions as negligence, requiring causation as described in the consent lesson. Hospitals may be liable vicariously for employees and, in the Darling v. Charleston Community Memorial Hospital (Illinois Supreme Court, 1965) line of cases, directly under corporate negligence for failing to supervise the quality of care.

Worked example. A radiologist misses a nodule visible on a chest film that a reasonably competent radiologist would have identified. The tumour is found a year later at a more advanced stage. The plaintiff must prove that the miss was a breach, through an expert, and that earlier diagnosis would more likely than not have led to a better outcome. If survival even with earlier diagnosis would have been under half, a jurisdiction following the traditional all-or-nothing rule denies recovery, while a loss-of-chance jurisdiction may allow proportional damages.

lessons.title: What Are Health and Disease? Naturalism, Normativism and the Limits of Definition
body: Medicine treats diseases, but there is no consensus on what a disease is. The question is practical. Whether something counts as a disease can affect whether insurers cover it, whether a person is excused from obligations, whether it is treated or tolerated, and whether a pharmaceutical company can market a drug for it.

Naturalism holds that disease is an objective, value-free biological category. The best-known version is Christopher Boorse's biostatistical theory. It defines health as normal functioning, that is, the performance of each part's typical contribution to survival and reproduction at or above a statistically typical level for a reference class, usually defined by age and sex. Disease is an internal state that reduces functional ability below that typical level. The theory has the advantage of separating disease from social values. Its difficulties are well known. Common conditions such as dental caries or, in some populations, gum disease are statistically normal but still seem to be diseases. Some reductions in function are unremarkable and not diseases, such as fitness differences. The choice of reference class can be disputed, and function in biology is a contested concept.

Normativism holds that calling something a disease is inherently evaluative: a condition is a disease because it is bad, harmful or undesirable, in a way that depends on human values. H. Tristram Engelhardt and K. W. M. Fulford developed versions of this view. The concept of disease on this account describes what we want treated. Evidence for normativism includes historical cases where conditions were classified as diseases because of social values. The standard example is homosexuality, which was listed as a mental disorder in early editions of the American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual and removed in 1973 after debate, a change driven by evidence and by shifting values. Drapetomania, a supposed disease of enslaved people running away, proposed by Samuel Cartwright in 1851, is another example of a spurious diagnosis serving social ends. Critics of normativism say it makes disease too subjective and relative.

Hybrid accounts combine the two. Jerome Wakefield's harmful dysfunction analysis says a condition is a disorder if it involves a failure of a mechanism to perform its naturally selected function (a factual component) and that failure harms the person according to social values (an evaluative component). Lennart Nordenfelt's holistic theory defines health in terms of the ability to achieve vital goals in standard circumstances.

Related terms help. Disease usually refers to a pathophysiological abnormality as understood by clinicians. Illness is the person's lived experience of feeling unwell, and sickness is the social role. A person can have a disease without illness (early asymptomatic cancer) and illness without detectable disease. The World Health Organization's constitution of 1948 defined health as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease, a definition criticised as utopian because almost everyone would be unhealthy most of the time. Proposals such as health as the ability to adapt and self-manage have been offered in response.

Practical consequences include medicalization, the extension of medical categories to ordinary experiences, and overdiagnosis, the labelling of conditions that would never have caused harm. The wider the definition, the more people are labelled.

Worked example. A student asked whether being shorter than 99 percent of peers is a disease would note that a statistical account says only that it is unusual, a normative account asks whether it harms or limits the person in context, and a hybrid account asks whether any underlying mechanism has failed and whether this harms. Growth hormone deficiency, caused by a failed mechanism, would count under the hybrid account, but idiopathic short stature without dysfunction is more contested.

lessons.title: Causation in Medicine: From Koch to Bradford Hill to Counterfactuals
body: Medicine constantly asks whether an exposure causes an outcome: whether smoking causes lung cancer, a drug causes a side effect, or a delay caused a death. Philosophy of medicine distinguishes several concepts of causation, because each fits some problems and fails others.

Koch's postulates, associated with Robert Koch and Friedrich Loeffler in the nineteenth century, set criteria for showing that a particular microorganism causes a particular disease: the organism should be found in all cases of the disease, isolated and grown in pure culture, cause the disease when introduced into a healthy host, and be re-isolated. They were influential and helped build germ theory, but they fail for many conditions. Asymptomatic carriers carry the organism without disease, some organisms cannot be grown in culture, and many diseases have multiple contributing causes. Koch's single necessary cause model does not fit chronic disease.

Sir Austin Bradford Hill proposed in 1965 a list of considerations for judging whether an observed association is likely causal. They are often called Bradford Hill criteria, but Hill himself presented them as viewpoints and not as a checklist. They include strength of association, consistency across studies, specificity, temporality (the cause must precede the effect, which is the only essential one), biological gradient or dose-response, plausibility, coherence, experiment, and analogy. The point is that causal inference is a judgment that combines evidence and does not reduce to a single test. The smoking and lung cancer case was the paradigm, since randomised trials of smoking were not possible.

Kenneth Rothman's sufficient-component cause model pictures a disease as occurring when a complete set of component causes, a sufficient cause, is assembled. A given component may belong to many different sufficient causes, and a disease can have many distinct sets. It explains why an exposure can be a cause of disease in some people and not in others, and why removing one component can prevent disease without being the only cause.

Counterfactual accounts define a cause as something whose absence would have changed the outcome: the exposure caused the disease in this person if she would not have become ill had she not been exposed. This underlies randomised trials, where the control group stands in for the unobservable counterfactual of the treated group, and it underlies the but-for test in tort law. Observational studies use methods such as adjustment, matching, instrumental variables and natural experiments, but they depend on assumptions about confounding that cannot be fully tested. A confounder is a factor associated with both exposure and outcome that is not on the causal path and so can produce a spurious association.

The distinction between population-level and individual-level causation also matters. A study may show that a risk factor raises risk in a population, but cannot show that it caused disease in a given patient. Law struggles with this when it asks whether an exposure caused a particular plaintiff's cancer, and often relies on a relative risk above two as a rough indicator that the exposure more likely than not caused a case, a rule of thumb that is itself debated.

Worked example. Observational data show that coffee drinkers have more lung cancer. Smokers are more likely to drink coffee, so smoking confounds the association. After adjustment for smoking, the association disappears. Temporality is satisfied, but the strength of association has an alternative explanation, so the causal inference fails.

lessons.title: The Epistemology of Evidence-Based Medicine
body: Evidence-based medicine (EBM) was defined by David Sackett and colleagues in 1996 as the conscientious, explicit and judicious use of current best evidence in making decisions about the care of individual patients, integrated with clinical expertise and patient values. The definition has three parts, and critics who say EBM ignores expertise and patients are often attacking a caricature. The philosophical questions concern what counts as evidence and how it supports a conclusion.

A familiar hierarchy ranks evidence from systematic reviews of randomised trials and individual randomised trials, through cohort and case-control studies, to case series and expert opinion. The rationale for randomisation is that it balances known and unknown confounders on average, so differences in outcome can be attributed to the intervention, and blinding limits expectation effects. Modern frameworks such as GRADE do not simply rank by design. They grade the certainty of evidence for each outcome, starting high for randomised trials and low for observational studies, then moving down for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias, or up for large effects or dose-response, and they separate certainty of evidence from strength of recommendation, which depends also on values and resources.

Philosophers have raised several challenges. Randomisation balances confounders only in expectation. In a single trial, particularly a small one, chance imbalances can occur. Nancy Cartwright and others argue that a trial establishes that an intervention worked in the trial population, but that applying it to a particular patient requires further assumptions about similarity, which is the problem of external validity or generalisability. Trials often exclude older patients, those with several conditions, and women of childbearing age. Average effects can hide heterogeneity, so a treatment that helps some and harms others can look neutral.

Other concerns include surrogate endpoints, such as blood pressure or cholesterol or tumour shrinkage, which are used in place of outcomes patients care about. A surrogate is valid only if effects on it reliably predict effects on the clinical outcome, and history has examples in which a drug improved a surrogate but did harm. The CAST trial in the 1980s and 1990s is a standard teaching case: drugs that suppressed ventricular arrhythmias after myocardial infarction, a favourable surrogate, increased mortality. Publication bias, selective outcome reporting and sponsor influence distort the literature, and trial registration and reporting standards are partial remedies. P-values and statistical significance are often misread, and the replication problem in science is a reminder that single studies are fallible.

Bayesian reasoning links evidence to diagnosis. The probability that a positive test indicates disease depends on the pretest probability, the sensitivity and the specificity, and for a rare disease even a very accurate test yields many false positives. Neglecting base rates is a common cognitive error.

EBM also has limits and complements. Mechanistic evidence, case reports for rare events, qualitative evidence about patient experience and expert judgment all have a role, and some interventions, such as parachutes in the famous satirical argument, are accepted without a randomised trial because the effect is so large and the mechanism so clear. Shared decision-making integrates evidence with patient values, where the best choice depends on how a patient weighs benefit against burden.

Worked example. A trial shows that a drug lowers a biomarker in men aged 50 to 65 with no other illness. A clinician considering it for an 84-year-old woman with several conditions asks about outcomes that matter, whether the trial population resembles her, and whether the absolute benefit, not just the relative reduction, is large enough for her goals.

questions.prompt: Which set correctly lists the four principles of principlism as set out by Beauchamp and Childress?
choices: Autonomy, fidelity, veracity and justice
Beneficence, confidentiality, justice and equity
Nonmaleficence, utility, justice and reciprocity
Autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence and justice

questions.prompt: What does it mean to say a principle is prima facie binding?
choices: It binds absolutely, so that the principle always overrides every competing consideration in medicine
It binds only when the patient has explicitly requested it, giving it no force without a request
It binds unless it conflicts with an equal or stronger duty in the particular circumstances
It binds only when no other clinician on the team disagrees about the right course of action

questions.prompt: Why do Beauchamp and Childress treat nonmaleficence and beneficence as separate principles?
choices: The two always recommend the same action in practice, and are only listed separately for emphasis
The duty not to harm is generally more stringent than the duty to provide benefit
Beneficence is a duty of physicians alone, whereas nonmaleficence is the shared duty of the wider team
Nonmaleficence is a legal liability standard, whereas beneficence is a purely aspirational ethical ideal

questions.prompt: A competent 58-year-old Jehovah's Witness with a bleeding gastric ulcer, fully informed that transfusion may be lifesaving, declines blood products and accepts other treatment. Her surgeon strongly believes transfusion is in her interest. Which analysis best reflects principlism?
choices: Autonomy is decisive because capacity and understanding are intact; the team explores her reasons, offers alternatives and respects the refusal
Beneficence is decisive because preserving life is the lexically first duty, so transfusion should proceed once she loses consciousness
Justice is decisive because blood is a scarce shared resource and her refusal commits the hospital to a costlier course, so it may be set aside
Nonmaleficence is decisive because withholding a transfusion is itself a harm, so her refusal is invalid without an ethics ruling

questions.prompt: A critic says principlism is "a checklist" that gives no way to decide when autonomy conflicts with beneficence. Which response from within the framework is most accurate?
choices: The framework resolves every conflict by ranking autonomy first, so no further weighing of the principles is required
The framework resolves conflicts by majority vote among clinicians, which is why it is called a consensus method
The framework concedes that conflicts have no rational resolution, so they are left to institutional policy or the senior clinician
The framework supplies specification and balancing, requiring explicit reasons for how each principle is weighed in the case

questions.prompt: Which moral theory is most associated with the idea that persons must never be treated merely as means?
choices: Kantian deontology
Classical utilitarianism
Aristotelian virtue ethics
Ethical egoism
