questions.prompt: A hospital board evaluates a policy purely by asking which option yields the greatest total improvement in patient outcomes per dollar. Which approach is it using?
choices: Narrative reasoning
Consequentialist reasoning

choices: A clinician's belief that a placebo has no effect on the participants of a trial, so that no participant can be misled about it
The mistaken view that a clinical trial can be run without ethical approval so long as every participant has signed a consent form
The belief that a drug which is already approved for one use cannot be studied further in any new population or indication
A participant's belief that research procedures are designed for her personal therapeutic benefit

questions.prompt: A proposed trial would randomise patients with a serious bacterial infection to a new antibiotic or to saline placebo, although an established antibiotic is known to be highly effective and withholding it risks death. How would an IRB most appropriately respond?
choices: Approve the design if participants sign a consent form accepting the risk of death or serious harm from untreated disease
Approve the design because institutional review boards may not weigh the scientific alternatives when assessing the risks to participants
Reject the placebo arm because withholding a proven effective therapy causes serious risk, and require an active comparator
Approve the design because placebo controls are always the most scientifically rigorous way to test a new drug, whatever the condition

questions.prompt: An interim analysis of a large cancer trial shows a larger benefit than expected in the treatment arm, and the data monitoring board is deciding whether to stop. Which consideration is most appropriate?
choices: The board should consult the sponsor's marketing department before deciding, since the commercial value of the drug is the key consideration
Stopping for benefit serves participants in the control arm but may overestimate the effect, so pre-specified stopping rules and sufficient events are important
Stopping early has no statistical consequences, because trial results are unaffected by when the analysis happens to occur in the study
A trial should never stop early for benefit, because the full planned sample size is always required before any conclusion can be drawn

questions.prompt: What does the National Organ Transplant Act of 1984 prohibit?
choices: The purchase and sale of human organs for transplantation
The donation of organs by living persons to family members
The transplantation of organs from deceased donors
The use of waiting lists in organ allocation

questions.prompt: Which distributive approach gives extra weight to benefiting the worst off, which in medicine often means the sickest patients?
choices: Ethical egoism
Prioritarianism
Strict utilitarianism
Libertarianism

questions.prompt: Which set lists the four conditions of accountability for reasonableness as described by Daniels and Sabin?
choices: Publicity, secrecy, majority approval and review
Cost, benefit, risk and appeal
Publicity, relevance, appeals and revision, and enforcement
Efficiency, equity, autonomy and enforcement

questions.prompt: A hospital in a surge has one ventilator and two patients with equal prognosis: a 28-year-old unemployed man and a 28-year-old prominent philanthropist who offers a large donation to the hospital. Which approach best fits mainstream allocation ethics?
choices: Give the ventilator to the philanthropist because his donation will help more patients later, so his survival has the greater social value
Give the ventilator to the unemployed man because his social contribution is lower and so he has the greater need for it
Withhold both ventilators because no ethical basis exists for choosing between two patients with equal prognoses and equal need
Decide by a fair procedure such as a lottery, since prognosis is equal and wealth or social status is not a legitimate criterion

questions.prompt: A crisis standards of care protocol excludes all patients with intellectual disability from ventilators regardless of individual prognosis. A disability-rights group objects. Which analysis is best?
choices: The categorical exclusion conflicts with disability-rights law and sound ethics, which require individualised assessment of the likelihood of benefit
The exclusion is acceptable because intellectual disability always reduces survival from respiratory failure, which makes the group a poor use of resources
The exclusion is required by the Americans with Disabilities Act in order to conserve scarce resources during a declared emergency
The exclusion is acceptable provided that the affected group is told about it in advance and given a chance to object to the policy

questions.prompt: Which US law requires drug and device manufacturers to report payments to physicians, which are published in a public database?
choices: The Stark Law
The National Organ Transplant Act
The Patient Self-Determination Act
The Physician Payments Sunshine Act, part of the Affordable Care Act

questions.prompt: What does the federal Anti-Kickback Statute criminalise?
choices: Any payment from industry to a physician for any purpose, including legitimate research, consulting under a written contract and speaking
The disclosure of conflicts of interest to journals by authors, since the statute treats disclosure itself as remuneration for referrals
Knowingly and willingly offering or accepting remuneration to induce referrals of items or services paid for by federal health programmes
Any physician ownership of a hospital or an outpatient clinic, since ownership always creates an improper incentive to refer patients to it

questions.prompt: What did the court hold in Moore v. Regents of the University of California (1990) about the physician's duty?
choices: A physician has no duties of disclosure about economic interests once the treatment relationship has formally ended with the patient
A physician must disclose personal research or economic interests unrelated to the patient's health that may affect professional judgment
A patient owns his excised cells as property and may sue for conversion whenever they are used in research without his knowledge
A physician may never use excised tissue for research under any circumstances, even when the patient has consented in writing

questions.prompt: A cardiologist who receives consulting fees from a stent manufacturer sits on a committee choosing which stent the hospital will buy. She discloses the fees and then votes. A colleague argues disclosure solves the problem. Which response is most accurate?
choices: Disclosure informs others but leaves the potential influence on her vote intact, so recusal from the decision is the stronger management
Disclosure eliminates the conflict entirely because the committee is now aware of it, so her vote may be counted without any concern
Disclosure is irrelevant because consulting fees from a manufacturer never affect the professional judgment of a clinician on a committee
Disclosure makes her vote unlawful under the Anti-Kickback Statute in every case, so she must resign her seat on the committee

questions.prompt: A systematic review finds that industry-sponsored trials more often report favourable conclusions than non-industry trials, even when risk of bias ratings look similar. A reader proposes explanations. Which is most consistent with the evidence on how bias can arise?
choices: The only possible explanation is falsification of data by every industry sponsor, since honest trials could never favour the sponsor's product
The pattern shows that independent trials are always unreliable, so only industry-sponsored evidence should be used to guide practice
The pattern arises only because industry trials enrol many more patients, which makes small effects statistically significant by chance
Choices of comparator, outcomes, analysis and reporting can favour the sponsor's product even without data fabrication

questions.prompt: Which term describes a patient safety event that reaches a patient and causes death, permanent harm or severe temporary harm?
choices: A latent condition
A therapeutic privilege
A sentinel event
A near miss

questions.prompt: In the Swiss cheese model, what does a "hole" in a layer of defence represent?
choices: A clinician who has been deliberately negligent and should be disciplined
A patient who refuses recommended care and so contributes to harm
A legal loophole that allows hospitals to avoid liability for adverse events
A weakness in a safeguard, which can align with others to allow harm to reach a patient

questions.prompt: Under a just culture framework, how should a recklessly unsafe behaviour be treated differently from a simple human error?
choices: Reckless behaviour, conscious disregard of a substantial risk, warrants discipline, while human error warrants support and system repair
Both should be treated identically, because the outcome of the event alone determines whether a clinician should be disciplined or supported
Human error should be disciplined and reckless behaviour excused if no patient was harmed, because the outcome determines the culpability
Neither should ever be reported or reviewed, because reporting discourages staff from working and so makes the whole system less safe

questions.prompt: A resident notices after discharge that a patient was given the wrong anticoagulant dose, which led to a minor bleed that resolved without lasting harm. The resident worries that disclosure will invite a lawsuit. Which approach is most consistent with professional guidance?
choices: Alter the chart so the dosing history appears consistent with the order, and avoid any discussion of the event with the patient
Disclose promptly with the supervising physician, explain what happened, apologise, describe corrective steps and report the event for system review
Say nothing because no lasting harm occurred, and disclosure would only cause the patient and her family needless distress and mistrust
Disclose only if the patient asks about the dose at a later visit, since volunteering the error would be an unrequested intrusion

questions.prompt: A hospital adopts a programme of prompt disclosure of errors, investigation and early offers of compensation. A critic predicts that claims will inevitably rise. Which statement about the evidence is most accurate?
choices: Evidence conclusively proves that such programmes always raise malpractice claims in every hospital, because patients learn of errors
Evidence shows that the programmes are illegal in every state that has passed an apology statute protecting the clinician's expression of regret
Some institutions report no rise in claims and possibly lower costs, though the evidence is mixed and the effect depends on context
Evidence conclusively proves that such programmes always reduce malpractice claims in every hospital that has adopted a disclosure policy

questions.prompt: Which four elements must a plaintiff prove in a medical malpractice claim?
choices: Notice, consent, breach and apology
Duty, breach, causation and damages
Intent, consent, causation and damages
Duty, motive, breach and punishment

questions.prompt: In which situation is the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur most likely to allow an inference of negligence without expert testimony?
choices: A surgical instrument is found inside a patient after an abdominal operation
A patient's cancer recurs after surgery performed by a skilled surgeon
A patient has a known complication of a procedure that was disclosed beforehand
A patient dies after a difficult operation on a very ill person

questions.prompt: What does a loss-of-chance jurisdiction allow that a jurisdiction following the traditional all-or-nothing rule generally does not?
choices: Recovery without any proof that the physician breached the standard of care, since the loss of a chance is itself the injury compensated
Recovery of punitive damages in all malpractice claims involving a delay in diagnosis, whether or not the delay changed the outcome
Recovery by family members who had no relationship with the patient and who are not recognised as survivors under the wrongful death statute
Recovery when negligence reduced a patient's chance of survival below fifty percent, even if survival was not more likely than not

questions.prompt: A 62-year-old man with chest pain is told he has indigestion and is sent home. choices: The plaintiff wins because res ipsa loquitur applies to every missed diagnosis, so negligence is presumed without any proof of causation
The plaintiff loses because emergency physicians owe no duty of care to patients who leave the department before treatment is complete
The plaintiff loses on causation because earlier diagnosis would not more likely than not have changed the outcome
The plaintiff wins in full, because a breach of the standard of care has been shown and breach alone establishes liability for the harm

questions.prompt: A surgeon performs a hernia repair competently, but the patient had consented only to a repair on the left side and the surgeon, finding no problem there, repaired the right side instead without any emergency or a further discussion. Which claim is most directly supported?
choices: A claim lies under EMTALA, because that statute governs consent to elective surgery and sets the standard of disclosure for operations
Battery, because the procedure was substantially different from the one to which the patient consented
No claim lies, because skilful surgery cannot give rise to any liability when the patient has signed a general consent form before the operation
Only a negligent nondisclosure claim lies, because battery requires an intent to injure the patient and the surgeon had no such intent

questions.prompt: According to Boorse's biostatistical theory, what is disease?
choices: An internal state that reduces functional ability below the species-typical level for a reference class
Any condition that society currently regards as undesirable or stigmatised, whatever the person's functional ability or underlying biology
Any state in which a person feels unwell, regardless of the underlying biology or of whether any function is actually impaired
Any condition that requires medical treatment in order to prevent death, so that conditions which are not life-threatening are excluded

questions.prompt: What is the best description of the distinction between disease and illness?
choices: Disease and illness are purely legal terms with no meaning outside the courts, which define them for insurance and disability claims
Disease is a pathophysiological abnormality as understood by clinicians, while illness is the person's lived experience of being unwell
Disease is a mild condition, while illness refers only to severe or life-threatening conditions that require hospital admission to manage
Disease refers to mental conditions, while illness refers to physical ones, so that the two terms never describe the same patient

questions.prompt: Which feature characterises Wakefield's harmful dysfunction analysis?
choices: A disorder exists whenever a person feels distress, regardless of mechanism and regardless of whether any biological function has failed
A disorder is anything listed in a diagnostic manual at the time of assessment, with no further condition about function or harm
A disorder requires both a failure of a naturally selected mechanism and harm as judged by social values
A disorder requires only that a person is statistically unusual in some trait, whether or not any function fails or any harm results

questions.prompt: A student argues that the 1973 removal of homosexuality from the American Psychiatric Association's diagnostic manual supports normativism about disease. A classmate objects. Which exchange best reflects the philosophical debate?
choices: The student says the removal proves disease concepts have no connection to biology; the classmate says that no diagnostic category has ever changed, so the example is not real
The student says the removal proves every diagnosis is arbitrary; the classmate says that it shows diagnoses are fixed by statutes passed by legislatures
The student says the removal was ordered by a court after a lawsuit; the classmate says the manual is itself a law of the United States

questions.prompt: A pharmaceutical company proposes that mildly elevated but statistically common blood pressure readings in a population be reclassified as a disease needing drug treatment. Which concern is most directly raised by the discussion of definitions?
choices: Medicalization and overdiagnosis, because widening a category labels more people who might not have been harmed
The need to abandon all disease definitions, since definitions can never be used for any practical purpose in clinical medicine
The fact that statistical normality guarantees that a condition is not a disease, so no common condition should ever be treated
The fact that normativism forbids any treatment of conditions that are common, since only rare conditions can be regarded as harmful

questions.prompt: Which of the Bradford Hill considerations is the only one generally regarded as essential for causation?
choices: Temporality, because the cause must precede the effect
Specificity, because each cause must produce only one disease
Analogy, because a similar cause must be known for another disease
Strength of association, because a weak association can never be causal

questions.prompt: Why do Koch's postulates fail for many chronic and multifactorial diseases?
choices: They require that no healthy person ever carries the organism, which is a condition that is always satisfied in practice
They assume a single necessary organism, which does not fit diseases with carriers, multiple causes or organisms that cannot be cultured
They allow causation to be inferred from any statistical association alone, without any experiment or specific isolation of an organism
They were developed to study drugs rather than organisms, and so they cannot be applied to infectious diseases at all

questions.prompt: What is a confounder?
choices: A random error in measurement that affects all subjects equally and that is removed by increasing the size of the sample
A variable that has been measured only after the outcome occurred, so that it cannot be adjusted for in the analysis
A factor associated with both the exposure and the outcome, not on the causal path, that can create a spurious association
A factor that lies on the causal path between exposure and outcome and explains how the effect of the exposure occurs

questions.prompt: An observational study finds that people who carry matches have higher rates of lung cancer than those who do not. Smoking explains both match carrying and lung cancer. Which statement best describes this situation?
choices: Match carrying is a mediator on the causal path from smoking to lung cancer, so adjusting for it would remove a real effect
The association shows that carrying matches is a sufficient cause of lung cancer, since the cancer occurs in those who carry them
The association proves nothing, because observational studies cannot detect any real causes and so cannot inform clinical practice
Smoking confounds the association, and adjusting for it should remove the apparent effect of carrying matches

questions.prompt: A court must decide whether a chemical exposure caused a specific plaintiff's cancer. An epidemiological study shows that exposure doubled the relative risk in the population. Which statement best reflects the problem of moving from population to individual causation?

Population data are irrelevant to individual causation and may never be used in court, since only direct evidence can establish a cause
A relative risk of exactly two proves that the exposure caused the plaintiff's cancer with certainty, since it is the legal threshold
Individual causation can always be established by examining the tumour under a microscope, which shows which exposure produced it

questions.prompt: How did Sackett and colleagues define evidence-based medicine in 1996?

The conscientious, explicit and judicious use of current best evidence in decisions about individual patients, integrated with clinical expertise and patient values
The replacement of clinical judgment by rules derived from randomised trials alone, whatever the patient's circumstances or preferences
The use of expert opinion as the highest form of evidence for medical decisions, ahead of controlled studies and systematic reviews

questions.prompt: What is the main rationale for randomisation in a clinical trial?
choices: It balances known and unknown confounders between groups on average so that differences can be attributed to the intervention
It guarantees that every participant will benefit from the intervention under study, so that no participant is disadvantaged by the allocation
It ensures that participants and clinicians both know which treatment was given, so that care can be adjusted to each patient
It removes the need for statistical analysis of the results, because chance can no longer produce a difference between the groups

questions.prompt: Why is a surrogate endpoint potentially misleading?
choices: Surrogate endpoints can only be measured in animal studies and so never apply to humans, which is why regulators do not accept them
Surrogates are always identical to the clinical outcome and so give no extra information, which makes them redundant in every trial
Surrogate endpoints are forbidden in all trials by regulatory agencies, which require that every trial measure death as its outcome
An effect on the surrogate may not reliably predict an effect on the outcome that matters to patients, and some treatments improve surrogates while causing harm

questions.prompt: A trial of a new antihypertensive enrolled adults aged 45 to 65 with no other illnesses, and showed fewer strokes. A geriatrician considers it for an 86-year-old with advanced kidney disease and frequent falls. Which concern best illustrates the problem of external validity?

The trial result is meaningless because fewer strokes is not an outcome of interest to patients and does not reflect any real benefit
The patient differs from the trial population in age and comorbidity, so the average effect may not apply and harms such as falls may weigh more heavily
The trial has no internal validity because it was randomised, so its results cannot be applied to this or to any other patient

questions.prompt: A screening test for a rare disease that affects 1 in 1,000 people has sensitivity of 95 percent and specificity of 95 percent. A patient with no symptoms tests positive. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: The chance that she has the disease cannot be estimated by any method, because the prevalence of the disease is not known to the clinician
The chance that she has the disease is still low, because false positives from the large unaffected group outnumber true positives

The chance that she has the disease is about 5 percent, because that is the false-positive rate of the test and it sets the predictive value
